The tech-heavy selloff left few corners unscathed : Memory-chip and data-center stocks got pulverized, with semiconductor shares taking their worst pounding in more than six years.

       2. TODAY’S HEADLINES   • Sen. Elizabeth Warren is about to take the controls of the Senate Banking Committee, giving her the kind of expansive authority over the financial industry she has long sought.

   • Texas Democrats stunned the world this week— and they are only getting started .

   • Israel’s most critical alliance is confronting its toughest test in decades after midterm elections brought to power more Democrats who question U.S. support for the country and led Republicans to call for a recalibration of the relationship.

   • Tuesday’s blue wave has left the MAGA faithful to digest a historic defeat while trying to imagine a future for their movement.

   • AI companies are scrambling to navigate a world hostile to data centers.

Computer-memory maker Sandisk won the dubious distinction of leading the S&P 500’s decliners, sinking by 22.3% Thursday. The silver medal went to Lumentum , which accepted a takeover offer earlier in the week. Unfortunately, it was an all-stock deal from another tech company. Maybe they should have insisted on cash. Get Spencer’s Markets A.M. newsletter in your inbox . 

   • Major investors are skeptical Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO can proceed as planned after a market selloff tied to the unwinding of AI-related bets, according to people familiar with the matter.

   • Millions of individual investors are learning the hard way what it means to have a concentrated stock portfolio. Two JPMorgan alums are staking their future on it.

   • A market rout in October walloped hedge funds , forcing them to unwind positions at the highest rate in years and cut staff.

       4. READ IT HERE FIRST   A drone maimed a Ukrainian army private. Could a drone also save him?   Trapped on the front lines of the war against Russia for nearly 500 days, Ukrainian army Pvt. Kostyantyn Vlasenko cut off his own foot to survive— until a daring mission rescued him by drone . During his time on the front line, Vlasenko played a critical role helping to blunt relentless Russian assaults near the city of Kupyansk, a key target in Moscow’s push to break the Ukrainian military. But for infantrymen, the biggest challenge is often getting out: Four men dispatched as replacements for Vlasenko were ki lled en route. Refusing to give up, his commander turned to a new kind of solution, attempting what Ukraine would later say was a first in the history of warfare: an evacuation by aerial drone. James Marson and Nikita Nikolaienko spoke with Vlasenko, his commander, Ukrainians involved in the rescue effort and a doctor involved in his care.

   5.   Democrats are hatching a plan to reverse Trump’s Canada tariffs.   Democrats are eyeing President Trump’s trade war with Canada as the first target in a campaign to roll back his administration’s tariff agenda, according to the party’s senior trade lawmaker in the Senate. Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the ranking member on the Senate Finance Committee, said there is “overwhelming support” for repealing the tariffs. The senator added that he was “already talking” with colleagues about legislation to push against Trump’s second-term levies after he gains control of the committee in January. Wyden’s statement follows an election season when many victorious Democratic candidates called for an end to the U.S.-Canada trade conflict, which threatens to intensify in the coming months before the new lawmakers are sworn in, reports Gavin Bade.

THE NUMBER   20%   That’s the share of students disappearing after placing their deposits at some schools nationwide, a phenomenon colleges call “melt.” The term refers to students who commit to an institution in the spring, then don’t show up in the fall . Amid enrollment pressures driven by a shrinking student population, colleges are implementing antimelt tactics—known as “freeze” strategies—to prevent competitors from poaching their committed students and to keep young people engaged with them throughout the year.

       9. AND FINALLY…   Hollywood’s new superhero is the guy who tells moviegoers when to pee.   We’re in the era of the ultralong movie. Some of this year’s biggest films, including “The Odyssey,” “Avengers: Doomsday” and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” clock in at nearly three hours. With no intermissions, viewers have to hold it or risk missing crucial moments. They’re flocking to RunPee, an app that recommends the best times for bathroom breaks with synopses of what they’ve missed. The service has been around for nearly 20 years, but it’s been adding new users. Since the release of “You Can See Everything,” around 7,000 people signed up to get advice on when to wrench themselves away from the marathon duel of unblinking eye contact between Holmes and co-director Nathan Fielder.

What the Midterm Shake-Up Means for Markets and Investors
 
Plus, Israel’s most important alliance confronts its biggest test in decades, and what’s next for Texas after the Democratic sweep
 
 
ALEX NABAUM FOR WSJ
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

The Republican drubbing in the midterm elections threw markets into chaos this week. The day after the election, energy stocks and oil prices tanked while consumer stocks shot up.

 

By Thursday, as the reality set in that voters swept a bloc of artificial-intelligence skeptics into power, Wall Street took another hit. The tech-heavy selloff left few corners unscathed: Memory-chip and data-center stocks got pulverized, with semiconductor shares taking their worst pounding in more than six years.

 

Common sense says to stay calm. As our Intelligent Investor columnist Jason Zweig writes, one of the most important principles of investing is to let your rules—not the headlines—make your decisions for you.

 

Before you check your portfolio, read Jason’s take on how to keep these wild swings from hijacking your financial future.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Sen. Elizabeth Warren is about to take the controls of the Senate Banking Committee, giving her the kind of expansive authority over the financial industry she has long sought.

 

• Texas Democrats stunned the world this week—and they are only getting started.

 

• Israel’s most critical alliance is confronting its toughest test in decades after midterm elections brought to power more Democrats who question U.S. support for the country and led Republicans to call for a recalibration of the relationship.

 

• Tuesday’s blue wave has left the MAGA faithful to digest a historic defeat while trying to imagine a future for their movement.

 

• AI companies are scrambling to navigate a world hostile to data centers.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

A drone maimed a Ukrainian army private. Could a drone also save him?

 

Trapped on the front lines of the war against Russia for nearly 500 days, Ukrainian army Pvt. Kostyantyn Vlasenko cut off his own foot to survive—until a daring mission rescued him by drone. During his time on the front line, Vlasenko played a critical role helping to blunt relentless Russian assaults near the city of Kupyansk, a key target in Moscow’s push to break the Ukrainian military. But for infantrymen, the biggest challenge is often getting out: Four men dispatched as replacements for Vlasenko were ki lled en route. Refusing to give up, his commander turned to a new kind of solution, attempting what Ukraine would later say was a first in the history of warfare: an evacuation by aerial drone. James Marson and Nikita Nikolaienko spoke with Vlasenko, his commander, Ukrainians involved in the rescue effort and a doctor involved in his care.

 

5.

 

Democrats are hatching a plan to reverse Trump’s Canada tariffs.

 

Democrats are eyeing President Trump’s trade war with Canada as the first target in a campaign to roll back his administration’s tariff agenda, according to the party’s senior trade lawmaker in the Senate. Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the ranking member on the Senate Finance Committee, said there is “overwhelming support” for repealing the tariffs. The senator added that he was “already talking” with colleagues about legislation to push against Trump’s second-term levies after he gains control of the committee in January. Wyden’s statement follows an election season when many victorious Democratic candidates called for an end to the U.S.-Canada trade conflict, which threatens to intensify in the coming months before the new lawmakers are sworn in, reports Gavin Bade.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

To cross the Red Sea, shippers email Houthi rebels. Read their inbox.

 
 
 

Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have effectively policed shipping in the Red Sea using an often-overlooked application system for captains seeking transit clearances. The process: Send the rebels an email. We reviewed the correspondence between shippers and the Yemeni militant group’s little-known clearance office.

8. THE NUMBER

That’s the share of students disappearing after placing their deposits at some schools nationwide, a phenomenon colleges call “melt.” The term refers to students who commit to an institution in the spring, then don’t show up in the fall. Amid enrollment pressures driven by a shrinking student population, colleges are implementing antimelt tactics—known as “freeze” strategies—to prevent competitors from poaching their committed students and to keep young people engaged with them throughout the year.

Hollywood’s new superhero is the guy who tells moviegoers when to pee.

 

We’re in the era of the ultralong movie. Some of this year’s biggest films, including “The Odyssey,” “Avengers: Doomsday” and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything,” clock in at nearly three hours. They’re flocking to RunPee, an app that recommends the best times for bathroom breaks with synopses of what they’ve missed. The service has been around for nearly 20 years, but it’s been adding new users.
